newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ATHLETICS-KIPTANUI GOES FOR YET ANOTHER WORLD RECORD.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-KIPTANUI GOES FOR YET ANOTHER WORLD RECORD.

text.p: Moses Kiptanui will go for the 3,000 metres steeplechase world record in Zurich on Wednesday to make up for the disappointment of missing out on a fourth consecutive world championships gold medal last week.
Kenyan Kiptanui, who was second to compatriot Wilson Boit Kipketer in Athens, is looking forward to the star-studded Swiss meeting where he has set two world best marks in the past.

"I'll run as fast as I can and it might be a world record," said Kiptanui, who clocked a world record of eight minutes 2.08 seconds here in 1992 and another one of 7:59.18 two years ago -- which still stands.
However, the 26-year-old said the Letzigrund track was never one of his favourites. "When I first came here in 1991 I fell. But since then I've been very lucky. Let's hope it will continue."
Kiptanui said he had mixed feelings about having lost his world title in Greece.
"Of course I would have preferred to win but it's not too bad because Wilson won it and it was a Kenyan 1-2-3. I was a bit disappointed for myself but very proud for Kenya."

Organisers have made sure that Kiptanui will have all the assistance he needs in his attempt for a third world record in this meeting where not only the track but also the unique atmosphere have so often produced fine performances.
"There will be some 10 Kenyans in the race and there will be a pacemaker," said Kiptanui.
"I don't really need a pacemaker to break a world record but if he runs really fast for the first kilometre, it might help. Then I'll just run my own race and we'll see what happens."
Kiptanui predicted that Kenyans would fill the top five places in the race, saying they were unbeatable.
"And it's not only steeplechase," he added. "I think that if the Kenyans were able to focus and train properly, they would dominate every event from the 800 metres to the 10,000."

He said the Kenyan federation was partly to blame because it did not always provide a suitable environment for the athletes and was responsible for a tough selection policy barring some competitors from entering major events.

"It's getting better but the problem is that some of those people don't know anything about athletics," said Kiptanui who trains in London with a group including several of Kenya's leading distance runners.
Kiptanui is also a coach who looks after compatriot Daniel Komen, the 5,000 metres world champion.
"If Daniel has recovered from his race in Athens, he might have a world record (in Zurich)," he said.
Kiptanui said he would carry on until the 2000 Olympics in Sydney, then concentrate on coaching.
"I am not that young anymore and my body will soon be asking for some rest," he said.
"I've had world records, I've been a world champion but I've never won an Olympic gold medal. That's something I really would like. After that, it will be time for a new life."
